title: Buttermilk pancakes
subtitle: Thick, fluffy American-style breakfast stack
excerpt: Buttermilk pancakes are thick, soft breakfast cakes leavened by the reaction of buttermilk with bicarbonate of soda. The batter comes together in about five minutes. Each pancake cooks in two minutes per side. The result is a stack of golden, cloud-soft discs that hold butter and maple syrup without collapsing.
sourceNotes: Fannie Farmer, The Boston Cooking-School Cook Book (1896), Project Gutenberg. Original recipe for griddle cakes with sour milk, the direct precursor of the buttermilk pancake. Marion Cunningham, The Fannie Farmer Cookbook (1979, later editions in the Marion Cunningham tradition) for the modern thick-stack version.

recipe.freezeNotes: Cooked pancakes freeze well between sheets of baking paper in a zip-lock bag for up to 2 months. Reheat in a toaster or dry pan.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The batter keeps in the fridge for up to 12 hours. It thickens as it rests; thin with a tablespoon of milk if needed.

glossaryTerms.definition: The process of introducing gas into a batter or dough to make it rise and lighten. In pancakes, bicarbonate of soda reacts with the acid in buttermilk to release carbon dioxide bubbles, which give the cooked pancake its lift and open crumb.

content.text: Buttermilk pancakes are thick, soft griddle cakes that get their height from the

reaction between buttermilk and bicarbonate of soda. The batter is mixed quickly and left to rest for 5 minutes: the bubbles form and set the internal structure before the pancake hits the pan. Do not overwork it.
Put {{plain-flour}} of plain flour, {{granulated-sugar}} of sugar, {{baking-powder}} of baking powder, and {{bicarbonate-of-soda}} of bicarb of soda and the salt in a large bowl. Whisk to combine.

In a separate bowl or jug, beat the 2 eggs with {{buttermilk}} of buttermilk and {{unsalted-butter}} of cooled melted butter. Pour the wet ingredients into the dry and stir with a fork until just combined. There will be lumps. Do not try to smooth them out. Leave the batter to stand for 5 minutes.
Heat a non-stick or cast-iron pan over medium heat. Add a small amount of vegetable oil and wipe out any excess with kitchen paper, leaving a thin film.

Pour about 60 ml of batter per pancake into the pan. It will spread to about 10 cm. Cook for about 2 minutes until bubbles appear across the surface and the edges look set. Flip once and cook for 1 to 2 minutes more. The pancake should be deep golden on both sides. Stack on a warm plate and continue with the remaining batter.

items.cause: Batter overworked, baking powder past its best, or buttermilk too cold.
items.fix: Mix until the flour disappears and no more: lumps are normal and desirable. Check that the baking powder is still active (it should fizz in warm water). Use room-temperature buttermilk.

items.cause: Pan too hot so the outside set before the inside cooked.
items.fix: Lower the heat to medium-low and cook the second side for a full 2 minutes.

items.cause: Too much oil or pan not properly pre-heated.
items.fix: Wipe out excess oil before each batch. Let the pan reheat between batches.

items.cause: Flour measured by scooping rather than spooning into the cup, or the batter has been in the fridge.
items.fix: Thin with a tablespoon of milk at a time until the batter drops easily from a spoon.

content.text: Blueberries pressed lightly into the batter just after pouring give the classic diner version. Sliced banana or chocolate chips work the same way. For a richer result, substitute half the buttermilk with soured cream. A teaspoon of vanilla extract in the wet ingredients is a good addition.

Buttermilk pancakes are the American weekend breakfast in the way that toast and marmalade is the British weekday one. The stack has been on diner breakfast menus since the nineteenth century, and Sunday pancakes is one of the most-shared cooking traditions in the United States. Maple syrup is the standard topping. The slight bitterness of the syrup against the mild tang of the batter is what the dish was built around.
